title: National-scale monitoring reveals widespread trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) contamination in UK surface waters
content: Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is a highly persistent and mobile, ultra-short-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) that is extremely abundant in the global environment. The accumulation of TFA in the environment is partly due to its capacity to form from numerous fluorinated precursor molecules, including pesticides, refrigerants and pharmaceuticals. TFA pollution is particularly significant in aquatic systems due to its solubility, although there is no UK-wide assessment of the state of TFA pollution in surface waters. This study assessed TFA concentrations in 214 water samples from all four UK countries (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) covering 54 sites across 32 rivers and 4 seasons. To understand the spatial patterns in TFA pollution, the relationships between TFA loads and various potential TFA sources were also examined. TFA was detected at 98% of sites, with mean and median concentration of 2210 ng L−1 and 201 ng L−1 respectively. Multiple TFA pollution hotspots were observed, including on the river Kelvin in Glasgow (maximum concentration: 78 500 ng L−1). Winter and spring were associated with elevated TFA mass loads, driven by higher flow in both seasons and higher concentrations in winter. Golf course exposure and intermediate arable land cover were significantly associated with higher TFA loads, possibly reflecting PFAS pesticide usage. However, our results also highlight the challenges of source attribution for a widespread contaminant with numerous sources, and we propose avenues for future investigation. Overall, this study provides an important baseline of TFA pollution in the UK and suggests prioritising precautionary action to prevent further emissions at source.
